_meta.note: The command line tool exists only in English by decision. The file exists anyway so that no user-facing text lives as a literal in code, and so every string can be reviewed in one place against part 5 of the glossary.

cli.usage:
Examples:
  bws list --query "start:auto !status:running"    what should be up and is not
  bws stop Spooler --dry-run --dependents          what stopping it would take down
  bws snapshot create before.json                  freeze the machine before a change

Usage:
  bws [-h|--help] [--version]
  bws list [--query TEXT] [--signatures] [--memory] [--follow-network] [--json] [--timing]
  bws stop|start|restart NAME [--dry-run] [--dependents] [--timeout SECONDS] [--json] [--timing]
  bws snapshot create [FILE] [--note TEXT] [--follow-network] [--force] [--json] [--timing]
  bws snapshot diff EARLIER LATER [--exit-code] [--json] [--timing]
  bws snapshot diff EARLIER --live [--exit-code] [--json] [--timing]

  --signatures reads who signed each binary. Several seconds, so it is off unless asked.
  --memory reads what each running entry's process is using. Fast, and off by default
  because it is a measurement rather than a setting: it is different a second later.
  A query about either turns that one on by itself.
  --follow-network lets the tool look at a launch path that lives on another machine.
  Off by default, and that default is about safety rather than speed: one unreachable
  share costs twenty one seconds, and the connection authenticates as whoever ran it.
  Without it the disk question for such an entry is reported as not read, never as
  missing, and the path itself is still shown.
  --timeout is how long the tool waits for one step to reach the state it asked for,
  counted from the moment the manager accepts the request. Sixty seconds unless you say
  otherwise. Running out of it is not a failure, it is the end of watching: the report
  says where the entry was left, and an entry left stopping usually arrives by itself.
  It is not a cap on how long the command takes. The manager answers in its own time,
  and for a service that never reports itself that answer takes tens of seconds - the
  report says so when it happens.

  snapshot create always reads signatures and hashes, because a snapshot is kept and
  compared later, and one without them would compare against one with them as though the
  machine had changed. Without a file name it writes into the current directory.
  --note says what the snapshot was taken for.
  --force writes over a file that is already there. Without it, an existing file is left
  alone and the command ends without writing - a snapshot is kept for months, and this
  will not replace one, or anything else, unless told to.

  snapshot diff says what changed going from the first file to the second. Configuration
  differences and running state are reported apart, because two snapshots taken a day
  apart differ in what was running and almost none of it is drift.
  --exit-code ends with code 5 when anything differs. Off by default, so a script that
  only wants the differences printed is not tripped by finding some.
  --live compares the file against this machine as it is now. It reads signatures and
  hashes, like snapshot create, because the file it is compared against has them.
cli.snapshot.fileExists: There is already a file at {0}. A snapshot is kept and compared later, so this will not replace one without being told to. Pick another name, or add --force.
cli.snapshot.quarantined: What was at {0} could not be read as a snapshot, so it was kept rather than replaced. It is now at {1}.
cli.snapshot.cannotQuarantine: What was at {0} could not be read as a snapshot and could not be moved aside either, so nothing was written. {1}
cli.optionNotForCommand: {0} does not apply to {1}. It works with: {2}.
cli.missingServiceName: {0} needs the name of a service. Example: bws {0} Spooler --dry-run
cli.badTimeout: --timeout takes a whole number of seconds, at least 1. It got: {0}
cli.plan.warning.cascade.one: Stopping {0} also stops one other entry: {2}
cli.plan.warning.inTheWay.one: One running entry needs {0} and is not included: {2}. The stop will be refused while it runs. Add --dependents to take it down too.
cli.plan.warning.inTheWay.many: {1} running entries need {0} and are not included: {2}. The stop will be refused while they run. Add --dependents to take them down too.
cli.plan.warning.sharedProcess: {0} shares its process with: {1}. Those keep running and the process does not go away.
cli.plan.warning.returnsAfterReboot: {0} starts automatically, so this lasts until the next restart of the machine.
cli.plan.warning.cascadeUnreadable: Could not read what depends on {0}, so more may stop than this plan shows.
cli.plan.warning.alreadyThere: {0} is already in that state, so nothing would change.
cli.run.interrupted: Interrupted. Finishing the step in flight, then putting back what was taken down. Another Ctrl+C leaves it as it is.
cli.run.abandoned: Leaving the rest undone. The report still follows, so you can see what was changed. Another Ctrl+C ends this without it.
cli.run.wasInterrupted: This run was interrupted. Steps that were never attempted say so above.
cli.run.outranTheCeiling: {0} took {1}, longer than the --timeout of {2}. That switch caps how long this tool waits once the manager has accepted a request. It cannot cap the manager's own answer, and here the manager took that long to answer - which it does when a service never reports itself to it.
cli.run.putBack.heading: To put the machine back the way this run found it, in this order:
cli.run.outcome.earlierStepFailed: not tried, an earlier step did not work
cli.run.outcome.cancelled: not tried, the run was interrupted
cli.plan.problem.notOperable: {0} is a driver. This tool shows drivers but does not start or stop them.
cli.plan.problem.cascadeNotOperable: Stopping {0} would mean stopping these drivers first: {1}. This tool does not start or stop drivers, so there is no plan it can offer.
cli.plan.problem.cannotComeBack.target: {0} is disabled, so restarting it would stop it and could not start it again. Set it to start automatically or on demand first, or use bws stop if stopping it is what you want.
cli.plan.problem.cannotComeBack.one: {2} is disabled and restarting {0} would stop it, so it could not be started again. Set it to start automatically or on demand first, or use bws stop if stopping is what you want.
cli.plan.problem.cannotComeBack.many: {1} entries this restart would stop are disabled, so it could not start them again: {2}. Set them to start automatically or on demand first, or use bws stop if stopping them is what you want.

cli.subcommandMissing: snapshot needs a word after it. There is: {0}.
cli.unknownSubcommand: There is no snapshot {0}. There is: {1}.
cli.snapshot.notElevated: Taken without administrator rights. The manager hands over fewer entries that way, so comparing this against an elevated snapshot will show entries as removed that nobody removed.
cli.diff.needsTwoSides: snapshot diff needs two sides: either two files, the earlier one first, or one file and --live to compare it against this machine.
cli.diff.liveTakesOneFile: --live compares one file against this machine, so give one file, not two.
cli.diff.notASnapshot: {0} is not a snapshot this build can read. {1}
cli.diff.uncertain: Cannot tell ({0}) - present in the elevated snapshot, and the other was taken without elevation, so the manager may simply not have handed these over:
cli.diff.notFullyCompared: Not fully compared ({0}) - nothing differs, and one of the two snapshots never read a field, so nobody can say either way:
cli.diff.field.incomparable: {0}: not compared, one of the two snapshots never read it
cli.diff.summary: Added {0}, removed {1}, changed {2}. Fields differing: {3} in configuration, {4} in running state.
cli.diff.summaryIncomplete: Not a complete comparison: {0} entries carry a field one snapshot never read, and {1} entries only one of the two could see.
cli.diff.caveat.elevation: The two snapshots were taken at different privilege levels. The one without administrator rights holds fewer entries, so what is missing from it may never have been removed.
cli.diff.caveat.machine: The two snapshots come from different machines.
cli.diff.caveat.operatingSystem: The two snapshots come from different versions of Windows.
cli.diff.caveat.tool: The two snapshots were written by different versions of this tool.
cli.diff.caveat.neitherRead: Neither snapshot holds these fields, so no entry was compared on them: {0}
cli.info.timingCompared: Read and compared two snapshots in {0} ms.
cli.query.unknownField: There is no field called {0}. Fields you can use: {1}.
cli.query.unknownValueNearest: {1} has no value {0}. Did you mean {2}? It accepts: {3}.
cli.query.badPattern: The expression /{0}/ could not be read. {1}
cli.query.unclosedQuote: A quote is opened and never closed, starting at: {0}
cli.query.badNumber: {1} expects a number like 1234, >1000, <500, >=100 or 100-200. It got: {0}
cli.query.emptyTerm: {0} says nothing. A ! needs something after it, and a word needs something in it.
cli.query.patternTooComplex: The wildcard starting {0} has too many parts to build. Use fewer * and ? characters.
cli.optionGivenTwice: Given more than once, and only one of them could be used: {0}. Say it once.
cli.diff.notUtf8: {0} is not UTF-8, and this will not guess at the bytes. A snapshot is written as UTF-8, so this file has been re-encoded somewhere - most often by an editor set to the machine's code page. Guessing would report differences that are not there.
cli.query.badSize: {1} expects a size with a unit, like 500MB, >1GB, <100MB or 100MB-1GB. It got: {0}
cli.warning.configurationRefused: Configuration was refused for {0} of {1} entries. Run elevated to read them.
cli.warning.delayRefused: The delayed start setting was refused for {0} entries, so they are shown without it.
cli.warning.queryIncomplete: {0} entries were judged on a field that could not be read. This result may be missing entries, or holding ones that do not belong.
cli.warning.queryTooCostly: The expression ran out of time on {0} entries, so they were never checked. Try a simpler one.
